citation.authors: Jing Huang, Atticus Geiger, Karel D'Oosterlinck, Zhengxuan Wu, Christopher Potts
citation.title: Rigorously Assessing Natural Language Explanations of Neurons

verification_method: Fetched 2026-10-20. The abstract page was read with WebFetch (title, authors, v1 date confirmed). The PDF was downloaded with curl and converted with pdftotext -layout; the two-column layout was de-interleaved by reading the extracted text against the PDF's structure. All quotes below are verbatim from the extracted v1 text.

claims.planned: The paper defines two evaluation modes for a natural-language explanation of a neuron: observational (does the neuron fire on all and only inputs the explanation picks out) and interventional (is the neuron a causal mediator of the concept)
claims.finding: Exactly as planned. The observational claim is formalized as: activation a(q) > 0 iff q is in the set of strings the explanation denotes. Type I errors are predicted-fire-but-did-not; Type II errors are fired-but-not-predicted. The intervention mode uses interchange interventions and interchange intervention accuracy (IIA), a variant of causal mediation analysis.
claims.quote: In the observational mode, we evaluate claims that a neuron a activates on all and only input strings that refer to a concept picked out by the proposed explanation E. In the intervention mode, we construe E as a claim that the neuron a is a causal mediator of the concept denoted by E.

claims.planned: They tested GPT-4-generated explanations of GPT-2 XL neurons from Bills et al. 2023, focusing on the highest-scoring explanations
claims.finding: They randomly sampled 300 (18%) of the 1.7k neurons whose Bills et al. score is at least 0.8. The abstract describes these as 'the top 0.6% of neurons which are considered well-explained by GPT-4's own assessment' (1.7k of about 300K). Test sentences were generated with GPT-3.5-turbo and manually verified; over 95% were valid.
claims.quote: We randomly sampled 300 (18%) of the 1.7k neurons whose explanations have a score of at least 0.8. ... We manually verified the correctness of the generated datasets. We found over 95% of the sentences to be valid.

claims.planned: Observational result: precision 0.64, recall 0.50, F1 0.56 for single neurons; random pairings score F1 of zero; F1 is essentially uncorrelated with the GPT-4 score
claims.finding: Table 1 (N=1, no probe): random 0.00, GPT-4 0.56. With learned probes over N=1 neuron, 0.60; rising to 0.73 at N=16 while the random baseline rises to 0.69, so the margin over random shrinks. The F1 score has a correlation of -0.1 with the GPT-4 simulation score.
claims.quote: For single neuron without probing, the GPT-4 explanations have a mean F1 score of 0.56 (with a precision of 0.64 and a recall of 0.50), whereas the random baseline has a F1 score of zero. With learned probes, the F1 score of GPT-4 explanations is 0.60. The F1-score has a correlation coefficient of -0.1 with the GPT-4 score.

claims.planned: They explain why a high simulation score does not imply a faithful explanation: the Bills scoring set is 5 top + 5 random excerpts, so a rare false positive is almost never sampled
claims.finding: Worked argument in the paper: an unfaithful explanation 'year 2000 and 2001' of a neuron that only fires on '2000' has precision 0.50, yet the probability of a Type I error appearing in the 5 random excerpts is about 1 - (1 - n%)^5, roughly 5n%, where n% is the corpus frequency of '2001'; for a long-tailed corpus that is tiny, so the score is insensitive to Type I errors.
claims.quote: The GPT-4 score is computed on a set of 10 examples from the GPT-2 XL training corpus, 5 containing tokens with top activations and 5 randomly sampled. We now show that an unfaithful explanation with a precision of 0.50 can still have a perfect GPT-4 score with high probability. ... the probability of having at least one example containing "2001" (a Type I error) is 1 - (1 - n%)^5 ~ 5n%. For any large corpus, n% could be extremely small due to a long tail distribution, which means the GPT-4 score is insensitive to Type I errors.

claims.planned: Interventional result: GPT-4 explanations select neurons with about the same causal effect as random selection; a token-activation correlation baseline does much better
claims.finding: Across tasks (unit conversion, numerical comparison, verb tense, capital retrieval), ranking by IIA gives: token-activation correlation baseline >> GPT-4 explanation ~ random baseline. The one partial exception is numerical expressions, which beat random but stayed far below the correlation baseline. No task was found where a single neuron's intervention changes behavior.
claims.quote: in terms of the IIA ranking, we have: token-activation correlation baseline >> GPT-4 explanation ~ random baseline. ... In other words, if we were using GPT-4 generated explanation to inform us which weights to modify in a model editing task, we would have similar performance as randomly selecting neurons to edit. ... We have not found a task where intervening on a single neuron can change model behavior in a causal manner.

claims.planned: They argue natural language is a poor explanation medium because of vagueness; many explanations use 'related to'
claims.finding: More than 30% of explanations in the Bills et al. dataset contain the phrase 'related to'; the paper gives examples ('mentions of pizza and related food items') whose denotation cannot be pinned down. Form-based explanations (spelling patterns) had precision 0.78 vs 0.62 for the rest.
claims.quote: More than 30% of neuron explanations in the Bills et al. 2023 dataset contain the phrase "related to". ... For Type I errors, i.e. precision error cases, we observe that form-based explanations have a higher precision at 0.78, while the rest only have a precision of 0.62.

claims.planned: Headline conclusion in the authors' words
claims.quote: We apply our framework to the GPT-4-generated explanations of GPT-2 XL neurons of Bills et al. (2023) and show that even the most confident explanations have high error rates and little to no causal efficacy.

teachable_points.point: An explanation is a claim with two halves (all, and only), and a test set has to be built to catch both failure types. Sampling random text catches neither reliably when the concept is rare.
teachable_points.quote: our observational testing regime is more reliable, provided the chosen experimental datasets have the potential to diagnose both Type I and Type II errors.
teachable_points.numbers: precision 0.64, recall 0.50, F1 0.56 on 300 top-scoring explanations; random pairing F1 0.00.

teachable_points.point: The two scores answer different questions and barely correlate; passing one is not evidence of passing the other.
teachable_points.quote: The F1-score has a correlation coefficient of -0.1 with the GPT-4 score.
